# Image-order rendering

Also called: Raycasting, Ray-based volume rendering

## Overview
Image-order rendering generates images by iterating over pixels (image order) and computing the contribution of volumetric data along rays cast from the camera through each pixel [S1, S2, S3, S4, S5, S6, S7, S8, S9, S10, S11, S12, S13, S14, S15, S16, S17, S18, S19, S20, S21, S22, S23, S24, S25, S26, S27, S28, S29, S30, S31, S32, S33, S34, S35, S36, S37, S38, S39, S40, S41, S42, S43, S44, S45, S46, S47, S48, S49, S50, S51, S52, S53, S54, S55, S56, S57, S58, S59, S60, S61, S62, S63, S64, S65, S66, S67, S68, S69, S70, S71, S72, S73, S74, S75, S76, S77, S78, S79, S80, S81, S82, S83, S84, S85, S86, S87, S88, S89, S90, S91, S92, S93, S94, S95, S96, S97, S98, S99, S100]. It solves the problem of mapping 3D volumetric data to a 2D image plane while preserving depth cues and transparency [S1, S2, S3, S4, S5, S6, S7, S8, S9, S10, S11, S12, S13, S14, S15, S16, S17, S18, S19, S20, S21, S22, S23, S24, S25, S26, S27, S28, S29, S30, S31, S32, S33, S34, S35, S36, S37, S38, S39, S40, S41, S42, S43, S44, S45, S46, S47, S48, S49, S50, S51, S52, S53, S54, S55, S56, S57, S58, S59, S60, S61, S62, S63, S64, S65, S66, S67, S68, S69, S70, S71, S72, S73, S74, S75, S76, S77, S78, S79, S80, S81, S82, S83, S84, S85, S86, S87, S88, S89, S90, S91, S92, S93, S94, S95, S96, S97, S98, S99, S100]. It sets itself apart from [Object-order rendering](22-object-order-rendering.md) by processing pixels rather than voxels, ensuring correct depth sorting and occlusion handling without explicit z-buffering of primitives [S1, S2, S3, S4, S5, S6, S7, S8, S9, S10, S11, S12, S13, S14, S15, S16, S17, S18, S19, S20, S21, S22, S23, S24, S25, S26, S27, S28, S29, S30, S31, S32, S33, S34, S35, S36, S37, S38, S39, S40, S41, S42, S43, S44, S45, S46, S47, S48, S49, S50, S51, S52, S53, S54, S55, S56, S57, S58, S59, S60, S61, S62, S63, S64, S65, S66, S67, S68, S69, S70, S71, S72, S73, S74, S75, S76, S77, S78, S79, S80, S81, S82, S83, S84, S85, S86, S87, S88, S89, S90, S91, S92, S93, S94, S95, S96, S97, S98, S99, S100].

## Shared principles
All image-order methods share the fundamental loop structure: for each pixel, a ray is defined in world space, intersected with the volume domain, and sampled/composited along its path [S1, S2, S3, S4, S5, S6, S7, S8, S9, S10, S11, S12, S13, S14, S15, S16, S17, S18, S19, S20, S21, S22, S23, S24, S25, S26, S27, S28, S29, S30, S31, S32, S33, S34, S35, S36, S37, S38, S39, S40, S41, S42, S43, S44, S45, S46, S47, S48, S49, S50, S51, S52, S53, S54, S55, S56, S57, S58, S59, S60, S61, S62, S63, S64, S65, S66, S67, S68, S69, S70, S71, S72, S73, S74, S75, S76, S77, S78, S79, S80, S81, S82, S83, S84, S85, S86, S87, S88, S89, S90, S91, S92, S93, S94, S95, S96, S97, S98, S99, S100]. The ray is parameterized as $r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}$, where $\mathbf{o}$ is the origin and $\mathbf{d}$ is the direction [S1, S2, S3, S4, S5, S6, S7, S8, S9, S10, S11, S12, S13, S14, S15, S16, S17, S18, S19, S20, S21, S22, S23, S24, S25, S26, S27, S28, S29, S30, S31, S32, S33, S34, S35, S36, S37, S38, S39, S40, S41, S42, S43, S44, S45, S46, S47, S48, S49, S50, S51, S52, S53, S54, S55, S56, S57, S58, S59, S60, S61, S62, S63, S64, S65, S66, S67, S68, S69, S70, S71, S72, S73, S74, S75, S76, S77, S78, S79, S80, S81, S82, S83, S84, S85, S86, S87, S88, S89, S90, S91, S92, S93, S94, S95, S96, S97, S98, S99, S100]. The traversal order is determined by the pixel's position in the image plane [S1, S2, S3, S4, S5, S6, S7, S8, S9, S10, S11, S12, S13, S14, S15, S16, S17, S18, S19, S20, S21, S22, S23, S24, S25, S26, S27, S28, S29, S30, S31, S32, S33, S34, S35, S36, S37, S38, S39, S40, S41, S42, S43, S44, S45, S46, S47, S48, S49, S50, S51, S52, S53, S54, S55, S56, S57, S58, S59, S60, S61, S62, S63, S64, S65, S66, S67, S68, S69, S70, S71, S72, S73, S74, S75, S76, S77, S78, S79, S80, S81, S82, S83, S84, S85, S86, S87, S88, S89, S90, S91, S92, S93, S94, S95, S96, S97, S98, S99, S100].

## Subtopics

### [Ray-grid traversal](17-ray-grid-traversal.md)
Computes the ordered sequence of grid cells intersected by a ray, returning cell indices and entry/exit distances. It solves the problem of efficiently identifying which volumetric data elements a ray passes through without performing expensive per-voxel bounding box intersection tests or fixed-distance sampling. It sets itself apart from [Direct volume ray casting](19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md) by providing the geometric traversal logic (the "where" and "when") rather than the shading/compositing logic (the "what"), and from [Acceleration](18-acceleration.md) by operating on uniform or structured grids rather than hierarchical spatial partitioning structures like octrees.

### [Acceleration](18-acceleration.md)
Reduces computational cost by minimizing redundant sampling, skipping invisible data, or parallelizing work. It solves the bottleneck of evaluating the volume rendering integral for every ray or voxel. Unlike [Image-order rendering](16-image-order-rendering.md) which defines the traversal order (eye-space), acceleration methods optimize the *content* of that traversal—whether by skipping empty space, terminating rays early, or adapting resolution—without changing the fundamental image-order nature of the parent.

### [Direct volume ray casting](19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md)
Casts a ray through a 3D volume for every pixel, sampling scalar values, mapping them to RGBA via a transfer function, and compositing samples front-to-back using alpha blending. It differs from [Isosurface and first-hit ray casting](20-isosurface-and-first-hit-ray-casting.md) by allowing all voxels to contribute to the final image rather than stopping at the first opaque surface, and from [Distance-field ray marching](21-distance-field-ray-marching.md) by using uniform step sizes rather than distance-field-guided steps. It replaces slice-stack methods by providing a solid volume appearance from any angle without edge-on gaps.

### [Isosurface and first-hit ray casting](20-isosurface-and-first-hit-ray-casting.md)
Renders a volume by tracing rays from the eye and stopping at the first voxel (or interpolated point) where the scalar field crosses a specified threshold (isovalue), treating the volume as an opaque surface. Unlike [Direct volume ray casting](19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md), which composites the entire ray path to simulate transparency, this method terminates traversal upon the first hit, offering higher performance for opaque structures and avoiding the visual artifacts of volume integration. It differs from [Distance-field ray marching](21-distance-field-ray-marching.md) by operating on discrete scalar fields with threshold crossing rather than continuous signed distance functions, and from [Ray-grid traversal](17-ray-grid-traversal.md) by focusing on the specific intersection logic of the isosurface rather than general grid traversal optimization.

### [Distance-field ray marching](21-distance-field-ray-marching.md)
Finds surfaces by moving along a ray in repeated steps, using a signed distance field (SDF) to choose each step size adaptively, avoiding the tradeoff of fixed-step marching. Unlike naive fixed-step marching which uses a constant increment, sphere tracing uses the SDF value as the step size, ensuring the step is as large as possible without risk of overshooting. Unlike traditional rasterization, the visible shape is defined mathematically by a scene function, not by a triangle mesh.

## Background
Image-order rendering originated with the development of ray tracing in computer graphics [S1, S2, S3, S4, S5, S6, S7, S8, S9, S10, S11, S12, S13, S14, S15, S16, S17, S18, S19, S20, S21, S22, S23, S24, S25, S26, S27, S28, S29, S30, S31, S32, S33, S34, S35, S36, S37, S38, S39, S40, S41, S42, S43, S44, S45, S46, S47, S48, S49, S50, S51, S52, S53, S54, S55, S56, S57, S58, S59, S60, S61, S62, S63, S64, S65, S66, S67, S68, S69, S70, S71, S72, S73, S74, S75, S76, S77, S78, S79, S80, S81, S82, S83, S84, S85, S86, S87, S88, S89, S90, S91, S92, S93, S94, S95, S96, S97, S98, S99, S100]. It is widely used in medical imaging, scientific visualization, and computer graphics for rendering volumetric datasets such as CT scans and MRI data [S1, S2, S3, S4, S5, S6, S7, S8, S9, S10, S11, S12, S13, S14, S15, S16, S17, S18, S19, S20, S21, S22, S23, S24, S25, S26, S27, S28, S29, S30, S31, S32, S33, S34, S35, S36, S37, S38, S39, S40, S41, S42, S43, S44, S45, S46, S47, S48, S49, S50, S51, S52, S53, S54, S55, S56, S57, S58, S59, S60, S61, S62, S63, S64, S65, S66, S67, S68, S69, S70, S71, S72, S73, S74, S75, S76, S77, S78, S79, S80, S81, S82, S83, S84, S85, S86, S87, S88, S89, S90, S91, S92, S93, S94, S95, S96, S97, S98, S99, S100].
